summary: Defines a profile of Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) for managing X.509 certificates in systems that follow the US Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite. It covers capabilities, configuration and operation of the components involved.

plainLanguage.summary: A rulebook for handing out digital ID cards when only a specific list of approved secret codes may be used.

how do clients request certificates under cnsa
subtitle: Managing certificates using NSA-approved algorithms and CMC protocol.

tldr.problem: US National Security Systems need a standardized way to request, issue, and manage X.509 public key certificates while using only CNSA Suite cryptographic algorithms, ensuring consistency across the government's certificate infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8756 profiles the Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) protocol to specify how clients, Registration Authorities (RAs), and Certification Authorities (CAs) interact when managing CNSA-compliant X.509 certificates, defining requirements for each party and the algorithms they must use.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can achieve CNSA compliance for certificate management by following precise requirements for certificate requests (initial enrollment and rekey), using CMC protocol structures, and ensuring all cryptographic operations use CNSA-approved algorithms (SHA-384, ECDSA/RSA for signing, ECDH/RSA for key agreement).

today: RFC 8756 remains the definitive CNSA Suite profile for certificate management using CMC within US National Security Systems and other government agencies managing high-value information. As organizations continue to deploy certificate-based security infrastructure and transition toward quantum-resistant cryptography, this RFC provides the standard framework ensuring that all certificate lifecycle operations—from initial request through rekey and renewal—use government-approved cryptographic algorithms.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 8756 profiles the Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) protocol to support CNSA Suite compliance in certificate management. CMC is defined in RFC 5272, RFC 5273, RFC 5274, and updated by RFC 6402; it provides a standard way for clients to request X.509 public key certificates from Certification Authorities (CAs), optionally through intermediary Registration Authorities (RAs). The profile applies to all US National Security Systems managing certificates with CMC, and is appropriate for other US Government systems processing high-value information.

Unlike RFC 8755 (which covers S/MIME secure email) and RFC 8603 (which defines certificate structure), RFC 8756 focuses specifically on the protocol interactions between certificate requestors and authorities. It defines what requirements clients must meet when requesting certificates, what RAs must do when intermediating requests, what CAs must do when processing requests and issuing certificates, and what clients must verify when receiving certificates back. The profile covers two main certificate management scenarios: initial enrollment (when an entity gets its first certificates) and rekey (when an entity obtains new certificates with fresh key pairs).
sections.plainLanguage: The CMC protocol is how computers ask the government's certificate authority for digital ID cards. This document explains the rules both sides must follow, using only the approved secret codes.

sections.title: CNSA Suite Certificate Management Framework
sections.content:
The CNSA Suite uses the same cryptographic algorithms across certificate management as in other applications: SHA-384 for hashing, ECDSA with P-384 or RSA (3,072 or 4,096 bits) for digital signatures, and ECDH or RSA for key establishment. When clients and authorities exchange certificate requests and responses, the CMC structures must be signed using these algorithms, ensuring that all steps of the certificate lifecycle use approved cryptography.

The profile specifies behavior in a three-party ecosystem: a client (the entity requesting a certificate, which may be an end-entity or a third-party acting on its behalf), a CA (the Certification Authority that issues certificates), and optionally one or more RAs (Registration Authorities that can batch client requests and vouch for them to the CA). Each party has specific responsibilities: clients must properly format requests using CMC structures and sign them with CNSA algorithms, RAs must validate requests and re-sign them for the CA, and CAs must verify authorization and issue certificates. The profile requires all signatures to use SHA-384 and either ECDSA-P384 or RSA with appropriate parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: Three players are involved: the computer asking for a card (client), the authority that issues the card (CA), and optionally someone in the middle who checks and groups requests (RA). All of them must use the same approved secret codes.

sections.title: Certificate Request Process
sections.content:
When clients request certificates, they must create a Full PKI Request encapsulated in a CMS SignedData structure, signed according to RFC 8755 (the S/MIME CNSA profile). The request includes a control sequence with transaction IDs and nonces for replay protection, and a sequence of tagged requests. Clients can use either PKCS#10 (traditional certificate request format) or CRMF (Certificate Request Message Format). Each request must include specific attributes: a keyUsage extension (specifying whether the key is for signing, key establishment, or both), and proof-of-possession of the private key by signing a structure with that same private key. For rekey requests where the subject name might be reused, additional controls link the new request to the old certificate.

If a client has no existing signature certificate (such as during initial enrollment), it can authenticate the request using a shared-secret distributed out of band from the CA, or it can rely on an RA to vouch for the request. The Identity Proof Version 2 control authenticates a shared-secret-based request using HMAC-SHA384. The POP Link Witness Version 2 control provides an additional protection mechanism against substitution attacks, also using SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA384. All of these controls are optional depending on the authentication method chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer formats its request (asking for a signature or key-sharing key), signs it with its private key to prove it has the key, and sends it either with a secret password or by asking the RA to vouch for it.

sections.title: Authority Processing and Certificate Issuance
sections.content:
RAs (if used) receive client requests, validate that they use only approved algorithms, and batch them together. The RA creates a new Full PKI Request encapsulating the client requests, signs it with the RA's private key (which must have an RA certificate), and forwards it to the CA. The RA-generated request must include Transaction ID, Sender Nonce, and Batch Requests controls in its control sequence. If the RA is authorized via an extended key usage (EKU) field or a CMS Content Constraints (CCC) extension, this is validated by the CA. RAs must reject any request using non-approved algorithms.

CAs receive PKI Requests (either directly from clients or from RAs), validate that approved algorithms were used, verify authorization (checking that signature certificates used to sign requests are valid and trusted), and issue certificates. The CA must reject requests that attempt to modify critical fields like the public key or key usage extension. When issuing certificates, the CA returns a Full PKI Response signed with a separate CA certificate (not the same key used to sign issued certificates). For successful responses, the signature must use SHA-384 and ECDSA-P384 or RSA. For unsuccessful responses, the CA signs using the same algorithm that signed the request. The CA returns newly issued certificates in the PKI Response, and the client must verify that the returned certificate's public key matches what was requested and that the certificate validates back to a trusted root.
sections.plainLanguage: If there's an RA, it collects requests from computers, checks they're using approved codes, groups them, and signs them to vouch for them to the CA. The CA checks everything again, issues new certificate cards, and sends them back signed by a special CA certificate. The computer checks that it got what it asked for.

sections.title: Security Requirements and Constraints
sections.content:
RFC 8756 includes several critical security requirements. Shared-secrets used for authentication must be randomly generated and securely distributed out of band; they must provide at least 192 bits of strength. Implementations must use quality random number generators for all random values, following guidance from NIST Special Publication 800-90A, FIPS 186, and RFC 4086. Proof-of-possession of key establishment keys is performed using digital signatures, not the key itself; per NIST guidance, a single key pair must never be used for both signing and key establishment (except for one-time proof-of-possession).

Authorization to sign requests and responses is indicated through Extended Key Usage (EKU) extensions in certificates: id-kp-cmcRA authorizes RAs to sign requests, and id-kp-cmcCA authorizes CAs to sign responses. RAs must securely authenticate their requests to CAs, and CAs must verify RA authorization. The POP Link Witness Version 2 controls protect against substitution attacks where an attacker might try to swap key pairs. Clients must reject any PKI Response that fails authentication, signature verification, or key validation, and local policy determines whether errors are logged or reported to console.
sections.plainLanguage: Passwords must be long and truly random. Every computer must have the power to sign things with its private key. Special certificate codes say who can sign requests and responses. If anything looks wrong, reject it.
